title: A War Without a Controlling Hand: Hormuz Flows Fall to 68% of Pre-War Levels, the US-Ukraine Alliance Cracks in Public, and Two Asian Chokepoints Harden at Once
subhead: This week the Iran war stopped being a regional story and became the global economy's core constraint: Hormuz traffic fell to 11.6 million barrels a day against a pre-war 17.1 million, Brent touched $110, and a hot US inflation print drove a 7.6% single-day collapse in Seoul. At the same time Washington throttled Ukraine's Starshield link and froze new Russia sanctions for 60 days, while China's Liaoning crossed the Ryukyu chain and North Korea resumed missile launches.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Two Governments, Two Stories, and a Third of the World's Oil Missing
sections.body:
The week's central fact is a number. Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera put Strait of Hormuz flows at 11.6 million barrels per day in the week to October 13 - roughly 68 percent of the 17.1 million bpd pre-war baseline. Brent touched $110 a barrel on Friday, its first time at that level since May, with prompt North Sea cargoes reportedly selling near $135 earlier in the week.

The route got more dangerous even as the rhetoric got more confident. A Singapore-registered container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near the strait on Wednesday after being hit by projectiles. Iran's IRGC said the container vessel hit a naval mine on an 'unauthorised and high-risk' route; a US official attributed the attack to Iran, likely by missile. On Saturday, the IRGC reported a second supertanker struck a mine, each vessel carrying roughly two million barrels, while CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper insisted the strait 'is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran.' UKMTO counted at least 12 vessels attacked in the week to October 16 - and warned most victims never report.

Diplomacy stalled on substance, not procedure. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Washington's answer to Tehran's seven conditions was insufficient and that the strait would stay closed until they were met. A drone struck the Nicaragua-flagged tanker MT Petro Dolphin near Sohar, Oman, killing two Indian sailors - an attack in the waters of the very state mediating the talks.
sections.whyItMatters: Both belligerents now describe an open, contested waterway in the same week, and neither claims responsibility for making it safe. That ambiguity is itself the deterrent: insurers and shipowners price a route where the attacker is officially disputed.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia's Airports and Aden's Palace: The Yemen War Becomes the Main Front
sections.body:
The Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia crossed from harassment into a sustained air campaign. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport was struck 20 times in two weeks, killing at least 20 people and wounding more than 370 across airports in Riyadh, Abha and Dammam - the coalition later put the Riyadh toll at 17 dead and 330 wounded since October 1. Terminal 4 was hit for a second consecutive day on Sunday, killing one and injuring 11, a day after a Terminal 3 strike killed 13. Schools moved online, Riyadh Metro shut stations serving the airport, and the civil aviation authority suspended operations until at least October 15. Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki cited a cumulative total of 1,104 ballistic missiles and 1,135 drones fired at the kingdom since 2016.

Saudi Arabia answered. The coalition struck the Al-Sahaba oil facility near Sanaa after warning civilians away, framing it as cutting 'vital supply sources'; the Houthis claimed a strike on an Aramco administrative building in the Eastern Province, where a limited fire broke out. It was the first time in this round the two sides hit each other's core energy assets within a single day. The Houthis also fired five missiles at the Al-Ma'ashiq presidential palace in Aden, killing five and wounding 16 - hitting the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government, with the prime minister present but unharmed. A Reuters analysis described the campaign's aim as pressuring Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman both in Yemen and to push Trump into easing the blockade on Iran.

The week ended with the war widening into the Arab world's largest armies. President el-Sisi called an emergency parliamentary session in Cairo to authorise him to approve any Saudi request for defence assistance, saying Egypt would 'carry out any measure to protect' the kingdom while insisting he was 'not speaking in order for us to fight anyone.' Egyptian forces have not fought in Yemen since the 1960s.
sections.whyItMatters: A non-state actor has shut the Gulf's flagship airport for days and can now hit the anti-Houthi government's own capital. If Egypt commits forces to Saudi territory, a Yemen-Saudi exchange becomes a wider Arab coalition war while Washington is already committed in Iran.

sections.heading: The Russia Waiver and the Ukraine Rupture: Washington Picks Its Priorities
sections.body:
Trump tried to buy down diesel prices with a partial truce. He announced an 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine on Sunday; Zelensky said the deal was 'news to me,' called it 'a disgrace' when Ukraine broke it days later, and the truce collapsed within 72 hours as Russia continued striking power plants. On Thursday Kyiv struck a refinery in Ryazan and formally abandoned the pledge.

Then came the sharper break. Reuters, citing US and Western officials, reported the order to slow Ukraine's Starshield satellite service came from inside the White House. Ukrainian drone operations slowed and commanders reported lost connections; Zelensky said Kyiv received no early warning of Russian ballistic strikes on its power plants and called the absence of advance intelligence 'absolutely unjust.' Defence Secretary Hegseth later welcomed a restoration of service, a sign the cut is being walked back - but the damage to trust is done.

On Saturday, Secretary of State Rubio confirmed a 60-day waiver of new Russia sanctions and tariffs, including restrictions Congress had just passed, justified on national-security grounds and framed as a window to 'analyze' the global impact. Moscow called it 'historic.' Zelensky said it rewards Putin; the Bank of England's Andrew Bailey walked out of an IMF session in Bangkok along with counterparts from France, Germany and the Nordic and Baltic states when Russia's finance minister took the floor.

Europe moved to backfill. At the Brussels summit, Zelensky asked for an additional 70 billion euros ($79 billion) for next year, saying the war will cost 155 billion euros in 2026. Council President Antonio Costa said, 'This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,' while Estonia's Kristen Michal warned 'this winter will be once again like hell.'
sections.whyItMatters: The transatlantic split is now operational: Washington throttles intelligence, eases Russian sanctions and strikes a diesel deal with Moscow, while Europe scrambles to fund an ally the US has just de-prioritised. Every Ukrainian winter decision now runs through Brussels, not Washington.

sections.heading: Two Chokepoints, One Week: The Liaoning and North Korea Move While Washington Looks West
sections.body:
Pyongyang opened the week by firing multiple ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast, ending a nine-day pause; SBS reported the projectiles flew more than 900km. Seoul's presidential national security office convened an emergency meeting. China simultaneously announced five maritime military exercises across the Bohai, Yellow, East China and South China Seas - and on Wednesday Japan's Joint Staff Office disclosed that the carrier CNS Liaoning and three escorts passed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako, then launched and recovered aircraft about 250km south of Ishigaki, its first public disclosure since May-June.

The transits overlapped with Keen Sword, the year's largest US-Japan exercise - and with a new US deployment: NMESIS and MADIS anti-ship missile systems on Japan's Yonaguni Island, roughly 109km from Taiwan, for the first time. Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te pledged a record NT$1.1 trillion defence budget; the PLA flew 12 aircraft and 9 vessels around the island that same period. Seoul then tested its first domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle, which President Lee Jae-myung called 'a new means of deterrence.'
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is rehearsing the exact chokepoint transit a Taiwan contingency would require, on an island chain where the US has just emplaced anti-ship missiles. Every move raises the cost of Washington being absorbed in the Gulf - and both adversaries have noticed.

sections.heading: The Economic Bill Arrives: A Hot Inflation Print, a 7.6% Kospi Crash, and a Divided G20
sections.body:
The war's cost reached portfolios on Wednesday. A hotter-than-expected US inflation reading - the fastest in five months, with elevated oil prices a cited driver - pushed traders to price more Fed tightening. MSCI's Asia-Pacific gauge fell 2.7%, South Korea's Kospi dropped 7.6% with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each down more than 9%, and the Russell 2000 entered a correction on Wall Street.

The real economy followed the markets. Iraq devalued its dinar to ease a cash crunch. G20 finance ministers meeting in Bangkok alongside the IMF and World Bank faced an agenda dominated by Hormuz disruption, with Australia's Treasurer Jim Chalmers calling for an end to the Middle East conflicts and the reopening of the strait 'because that's what the global economy desperately needs.' US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not attend, citing 'domestic engagements.'
sections.whyItMatters: The transmission channel from the Gulf to ordinary households is now the Fed's rate path, not just the pump price. A 7.6% single-day Kospi fall shows how leveraged the AI-driven rally was to a benign inflation outlook - and how fast that assumption can break.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Eritrea: A War Narrowly Avoided, a Crisis Left Open
sections.body:
The week began with the Horn of Africa sliding toward open interstate war. Eritrean troops moved deep into Tigray, with Ethiopia formally accusing Asmara of an invasion reaching up to 60km and estimating the deployment at roughly 6,000 troops; Eritrea asked the UN Security Council to condemn what it called a 'declaration of war.' The International Crisis Group warned on October 12 that the two were 'edging closer to a direct conflict.' ACLED reported drones targeting Eritrean troops inside Ethiopia, implying external supply chains.

Ethiopian forces retook Adigrat after Eritrean troops withdrew under heavy drone strikes, and federal forces pushed back a TPLF uprising that began in September. By Friday Abiy Ahmed had installed a six-month caretaker administration in Tigray with five appointees carrying out directives issued directly from Addis Ababa, promising elections at the end of it. Eritrea severed diplomatic ties entirely; Ethiopia closed its embassy and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats. Secretary of State Rubio called Abiy to press de-escalation and cited the 2018 peace framework as the only sustainable path.
sections.whyItMatters: A caretaker administration appointed from the capital is a claim of control, not a settlement - the TPLF has not agreed to it. The 2020-2022 war killed nearly 600,000 people, and the grievances behind it are now stacked under a government with no diplomatic channel to Asmara.

sections.heading: The Rest of the Map: Nuclear Talks, NATO's Turkish Lock, Pakistan, and Gaza
sections.body:
With the last US-Russia arms treaty expired, Trump told Newsmax the US is in denuclearisation talks with both Russia and China - unverified, and likely aspirational, given Beijing's repeated refusal to join a US-Russia framework. Russia and the US hold an estimated 86 percent of the world's nuclear weapons; China's arsenal is about 620 warheads, per SIPRI. Macron responded with a Forward Deterrence Initiative. In the Middle East, Wang Yi told Israel's president in Baku to reverse West Bank settlements, calling the Palestinian question 'the greatest historical injustice of this century' - while China buys up to 90 percent of Iran's oil.

NATO called an emergency session on Black Sea security after drones struck ships in Bulgarian and Romanian territorial waters, with at least seven crew missing; any allied naval response is blocked by Turkey's refusal under the Montreux Convention to admit warships. In Pakistan, the federal government imposed emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, detaining PTI assembly speaker Sohail Afridi, while striking inside Afghanistan; the week ended with a school roof collapse in the province killing 33. In Gaza, the health ministry said malnutrition reached 'catastrophic' levels - at least 466 deaths since 2024, a third of them children - as Israel halted commercial goods and UNICEF counted more than 340 children killed in the year since the ceasefire was announced. Masked settlers attacked a European diplomatic delegation during the olive harvest, and Trump-appointed ambassador Mike Huckabee called a separate attack on an American journalist a 'despicable act of terror.'
sections.whyItMatters: Each of these is a separate file, but they share a pattern: the institutions built to contain them - arms treaties, NATO, provincial government, humanitarian truces - are failing at the same time, and the actors best placed to restrain them are distracted or unwilling.

bottomLine: This week the Iran war stopped being a Gulf story and became the global economy's binding constraint: Hormuz is running at 11.6 million barrels a day against a pre-war 17.1 million, Brent touched $110, and war-inflated oil helped drive a US inflation print that wiped 7.6% off the Kospi in a day. Meanwhile Washington is spending its leverage elsewhere - throttling Ukraine's Starshield link, waiving new Russia sanctions for 60 days, and floating the largest non-nuclear bomb as an Iran option while ruling out ground troops - which is precisely why Kyiv is asking Brussels for $79 billion and Europe's finance chiefs walked out on Moscow in Bangkok. Next week, watch four numbers: whether Hormuz flows recover above 13 million bpd, whether Trump's 60-day Russia waiver is reversed under bipartisan pressure, whether Egypt formally puts forces behind Saudi Arabia, and whether the Liaoning repeats its Ryukyu transit during Keen Sword.
